en: Annotated Ritual for Reciting the Bodhisattva Precepts Every Half-Month Commentary by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Vimalaratnagāyabhadra-mahāmudrātiṣṭha-sūtra (Vibhūtiratnagāyabhadra-mahāmudrātiṣṭha-sūtra)
Regarding this recitation format, the author remains unknown. Examining its beginning and end, it largely records passages from the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*.
Now, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* was translated by the Dharma Master Dharmakṣema during the Northern Liang dynasty;
as for the Sarvāstivāda *vinaya-mātṛkā*, it was [translated] by Yijing in the fourth year of the Jinglong era of the Great Tang.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master by Imperial Decree. Regarding the statement in the text of this Preface to the Precepts, "during the Semblance Dharma" (*sāṃketika-dharma*):

this refers to the period of one thousand years following the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during which the teaching spread to the land of Han. From the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty until the *xīnmǎo* year of the reign of Emperor Rénzōng of the Sòng dynasty, the teaching covered this soil for one thousand years;
this period is termed the "Semblance Dharma. All periods subsequent to this are termed the "Final Dharma" (*paścima-dharma*).
Regarding the Dharma: since it states "within the Semblance Dharma," it is clear that this was not composed during the Final Dharma period.

Furthermore, as the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* was translated later, this work could not have been compiled during the Tang dynasty; rather, it must be a compilation by followers of the Tiantai teachings from the late Tang or early Song periods.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of recitation should be appointed to recite it. Once the assembly has gathered like clouds, first perform the incense praise (*gandhapraśaṃsā*).
Having completed this, recite three times:
"Namo to the Buddha Vairocana, the Teacher of the Brahmajāla Sūtra."
Next, the verse for opening the sutra is recited. The one who recites it ascends the seat and addresses the assembly, saying:

"I, [Name], prostrate and pay homage. I respectfully inform the great assembly: I have been appointed by the Sangha to recite the precepts; fearing that there may be errors, I pray that those who join me in the recitation will compassionately point out my mistakes."
1. Initial homage to the Triple Gem; 2. Exhortation to practice; 3. Performing the preliminary preparations;
4. Reciting the preface to the Pratimokṣa; 5. The formal inquiry; 6. The actual recitation of the Pratimokṣa Sūtra.
First, having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, the assembly of Bodhisattva precepts, and so forth, listen attentively!
We take refuge in Vairocana and the Vajra Buddhas of the ten directions; we also pay homage to the former master of this treatise and to the Honored One Maitreya, who shall awaken [to Buddhahood].
Now I shall explain the three clusters of precepts; may all Bodhisattvas listen together.
In the Sanskrit language, *namas* means "to take refuge" or "to pay homage. *Vairocana* means "Pure and Perfect."
This is the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha; for a detailed explanation, refer to the commentary. Regarding the "Vajra Buddhas of the ten directions":
in all worlds throughout the ten directions, all Buddhas enter the Vajra Samādhi, sever the final subtle ignorance, and attain perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
This refers to the realization of the indestructible nature immediately following the Vajra Path. It is called such from the perspective of its functional capacity. Thus it says:

Regarding the term "Vajra," it is called "Buddha" from the perspective of what has been realized; "Buddha" means "Awakened. The Sanskrit name Maitreya is translated here as "Maitreya" (the Compassionate One).
Bodhisattva Maitreya left the household life under the Buddha and composed various Mahāyāna treatises, such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and others.
Later generations followed his teachings, such as the Bodhisattvas Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna. Therefore, he is so called.

Maitreya Bodhisattva serves as the primary author of the preceding treatise. In the tenth minor kalpa hereafter, when the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years, he will descend to birth and attain Buddhahood;

thus it is said: "The Honored One Maitreya shall awaken. (As one is about to recite the precepts, one first takes refuge in the Triple Gem to seek their empowerment. Regarding the three clusters of precepts (*tri-vidha-saṃvara*):
first is the precept of restraining conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), which means there is no precept that is not upheld. Precepts serve to prevent wrongdoing and cease transgression.

"Evil" means that which is unwholesome. Second is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): there is no wholesome quality that is not cultivated. "Wholesome" refers to the extensive cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices.
Third is the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): there is no sentient being who is not delivered. Now, these fifty-eight precepts can sever all evils;
this is precisely the precept of restraining the body, speech, and mind (*saṃvara-śīla*). By severing evil, one is then able to accomplish all [wholesome qualities].
"Good. This refers to the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). When evil is severed and goodness is perfected, one is then able to benefit sentient beings;
this is the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). All dharmas are fully encompassed by these three, and thus they are called a "collection" (*saṃgraha*).

However, the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) primarily governs internal virtue, while gathering sentient beings belongs to external transformation. Gathering virtuous dharmas encompasses both the internal and the external; it is through the internal...

Cultivate yourself well and guide others with goodness; this is to transform sentient beings below, cultivate myriad virtues in the middle, and thereby exhaust evil and perfect goodness to attain the supreme fruit of Buddhahood above.
Thus, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* says: "In teaching and transforming sentient beings, always remain free from weariness;
when virtuous karma is perfected, one will swiftly realize the Way of the Buddha. This is what the Buddhas of the ten directions [teach].
This is the Jewel of the Buddha. Maitreya Bodhisattva is the Jewel of the Mahāyāna Saṃgha. The three groups of precepts are the Dharma-Jewel of the Mahāyāna.
"All you bodhisattvas, listen together"—this is the exhortation for the assembly to listen to the precepts; that is to say, for those present before them.
All of you, listen with single-minded attention; having listened, reflect; having reflected, practice.
The precepts are like a great bright lamp, able to dispel the darkness of the long night. The precepts are like a true jewel mirror, illuminating all phenomena without exception.
The precepts are like a mani jewel; they rain down things to relieve poverty. One leaves the world and swiftly attains Buddhahood—this Dharma alone is supreme.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should diligently protect and uphold them.
The above passage is from the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, which speaks of the "Great Precepts of the Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi-mahā-śīla*).

Because they can shatter the ignorant darkness of beginningless birth-and-death (*saṃsāra-avidyā*), they are like a bright lamp of the world. Since they are able to destroy the ignorance of birth-and-death, they constitute the *saṃvara-śīla* (the precept of restraint).
These precepts are capable of distinguishing and regulating all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena through observance (*dhāraṇa*) and transgression (*āpatti*).
This analysis is exhaustive. Thus, it is like a precious mirror of the world, in which both beauty and ugliness are fully revealed. Therefore, the *Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra* says:

"Just as when a person looks into a mirror, they experience joy or sorrow based on what is beautiful or ugly; so too, by being able to eliminate evil and accumulate good, one clearly perceives the merits and wisdom of the Buddha-ground.
This is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). In the Sanskrit language, this is called *maṇi*; here [in Chinese], it is translated as "like..."
The Cintāmaṇi is the king of all jewels. It emerges from the palace of the Dragon King;

if a person obtains it and places it atop a *dhvaja* (stupa-pole), then according to whatever the sentient beings desire, it immediately rains down all kinds of gold, silver, the seven treasures, various musical instruments, and other such objects.
Now, this Dharma of the precepts gives birth to immeasurable supreme concentrations and wondrous wisdom, as well as all virtues.
The noble wealth of the Dharma rescues all sentient beings who suffer from the famine of lacking the Dharma; thus, it is like a worldly *maṇi* jewel that can relieve poverty.
Because it can rain down the noble wealth of the Dharma, it relieves the poverty of the nine realms; this is precisely the morality of gathering in sentient beings.
This right morality of the mind-ground is the sublime artifice within the methods for transcending birth and death, leading swiftly to the realization of Buddhahood.
This is the most essential point for awakening. Therefore, the *Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra* states: "Among all the various codes of discipline, the Sūtra on Precepts is supreme.
That [sūtra] is called supreme among the human, celestial, Śrāvaka, and Hīnayāna teachings;

this [teaching], however, is supreme among the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna teachings by virtue of the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-vidha-śīla*). Thus it says: "One leaves the world and swiftly attains Buddhahood; only through this Dharma."

It is supreme. For this reason, since one knows that these precepts possess the aforementioned powers and functions, one should diligently protect and uphold them, ensuring that no deficiency or transgression occurs.
II. Encouraging the Cultivation of All Venerable Ones: The spring equinox in the fourth month constitutes one season.

According to worldly convention, there are four seasons in a year; according to the Buddha-dharma, there are three seasons in a year, with the autumn season excluded. Of this [autumn], there are two [aspects].
Regarding the meaning: first, because the Buddha sought to shatter his disciples' attachment to permanence, he did not mention autumn.
Since autumn is the season of harvest when all things bear fruit, people reckon it as permanent and pleasurable; to destroy this clinging, he did not speak of autumn.

Second, the Buddha established the month of Kārttika to open the possibility for a later *anvāraka* (summer retreat), so that those undertaking the later retreat could continue their observances and achieve its completion.

It is called "sitting through the summer" (*zàxià*), not "sitting through the autumn. For this reason, one departs during the autumn season. As for the current statement that the fourth month is the spring equinox: from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month is termed the "spring period" (*chūnfēn*); from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is termed the "summer period" (*xiàfēn*). From... [the ninth month]... [is termed the autumn period]. From... [the tenth month]... [is termed the winter period]. Thus, it is said that the four months of the summer are the time for sitting in meditation. Regarding the phrase "the three months of the summer": the first month of summer is the fifth month; the second month of summer is the sixth month; the third month of summer is the seventh month. These three months are collectively called the summer. It is for this reason that the term "summer retreat" (*zhǎiyī*) is established. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the three months of the summer": the first month of summer is the fifth month; the second month of summer is the sixth month; the third month of summer is the seventh month. From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is called the winter period (*hemanta*).

Here, we first designate the spring equinox (*viṣuvat*), and the latter two periods should be adjusted according to the seasons. (Kārttika—this refers to the constellation Puṣya; because the moon is in conjunction with Puṣya during this month, it corresponds to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month.)

When half a month has passed, the end of the twelfth month constitutes one half-month; the fifteenth day of the first month constitutes one full month; the end of the first month constitutes one and a half months;
the fifteenth day of the second month constitutes two months; the end of the second month constitutes two and a half months; the fifteenth day of the third month...
Three months constitute one season; when three months have elapsed, it becomes the middle month of that season. The fifteenth day of the fourth month constitutes the fourth month.
For the remaining two seasons of summer and winter, apply this same principle accordingly.
One night is lacking; there remains one night and three and a half months.
"One night is lacking" refers to the end of the twelfth month; the *poṣadha* is performed during the day because this very night still belongs to the current day.
Because the night has not yet been completed, it is called "short. As for the phrase "one night remains," this means that because it is not yet finished, one night still remains.
If the *poṣadha* is held during the first watch or the middle watch of the night, one should say, "half a night is short; half a night remains.
The Buddha did not permit the *poṣadha* to be held during the last watch, fearing that the ceremony might not be concluded before the dawn appears.
Thus, for two days to share a single *poṣadha* constitutes an illegal act. If the *poṣadha* is on the fifteenth day of the first month, one should say:
"One night is lacking; there remains one night and three months. For all subsequent fortnightly *poṣadhas*, only the latter phrase is changed;
for example, if the *poṣadha* is at the end of the first month, it is changed to: "Two and a half months remain. 2.
On the fifteenth day of the month, one should say: "Two months remain. At the end of the second month, one should say:
"One and a half months remain. On the fifteenth day of the third month, one should say: "One month remains. At the end of the third month, one should say: "Half a month remains.
There may be those who, being ignorant of the Buddha’s regulations, instruct others that when encountering a minor (intercalary) month *poṣadha*, one may simply say "one less."
As for the night: if it were as large as the moon, there would be no need to mention it. If that were so, why mention only one less night rather than also one less day?

One should simply state directly that "one day is lacking. The preceding phrase should say "fourteen days have already passed," and only the subsequent phrase should speak of "one night being lacking.
However, the legal codes established by various nations differ, and thus the length of the months also varies.
It is not fixed; it simply follows the month-name [of the lunar calendar], regardless of whether it is large or small. This is because it would otherwise disrupt the regular order.
For example, when there is an intercalary month, one still refers to it by the name of the first month. If one did not follow the primary month, there would be five months in a single season.

Old age and death are drawing near; the Buddha-dharma is about to perish. O Venerable Ones, for the sake of attaining the Way, you laymen and laywomen should single-mindedly and diligently seek progress.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, through single-minded and diligent seeking of progress, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
how much more so regarding other wholesome dharmas of the Path! Each of you, while still strong and healthy, [should strive].
At this time, strive diligently to cultivate goodness; why not seek the Path? How can one wait until old age? What pleasure could there be [in doing so]?
From the spring equinox until now—this is the text of the Śrāvaka-vinaya of the Sarvāstivāda school. Now, the two assemblies of lay followers have been added here;
if these two assemblies are absent, it is not necessary to recite this text. This applies, for example, in the case of śrāmaṇeras, bodhisattvas, and others.
One should address them as "Venerable Sirs. According to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one should instead call them "Great Beings" (*mahāsattva*).
Regarding the phrase "old age and death are near," this refers to how many months and days have already passed and how many months and days remain;
it is intended precisely to awaken one to the passage of time and the approaching proximity of old age and death—namely, that as days go by and months come, one suddenly becomes white-haired.

It is thus: impermanence, old age, and death do not wait for an appointment with anyone. When the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, if one does not rely upon the precepts to advance in practice, the True Dharma will then vanish.
Once the True Dharma has vanished, where else can one go to cultivate? Therefore, the Vinaya says:
When there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*, then the True Dharma has not yet perished in the world.

The *Vinaya-piṭaka* is the life-force of the Buddha’s teachings; as long as the *Vinaya-piṭaka* abides, the Buddha’s teachings also abide, along with all wholesome dharmas, supreme meditative concentrations, and sublime wisdom.
All are produced by relying upon the precepts. Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (the last three characters of "Anuttara" should be preceded by the *kṣa* [ṅka] diacritic).
*Anuttara* here means "unsurpassed. *Samyak* here means "right. *Saṃbodhi* here means "perfect enlightenment."

This is precisely the unsurpassed path of the Buddha. As for other virtuous paths and dharmas, these refer to the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the path (*mārga*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and samādhis, as well as the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the human and celestial realms. Therefore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"By means of heedfulness (*apramāda*), one will certainly realize the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; how much more so the remaining virtuous qualities of awakening."
"Each of you has heard [it] while in good health" means that each of you has now been able to hear and recite this Dharma of the precepts.
You should take advantage of this time when body and mind are strong and healthy to strive diligently in the cultivation of all virtues. "How? is a word used to pose a counter-question.
This means that having already heard the Dharma of the precepts, why not seek to advance in the practice of the path?

How could one remain complacent, simply waiting until the end of life when one has grown old and infirm, unable to practice further, with the day of death drawing near? What kind of pleasure would one then seek?
Therefore, it is asked: "What pleasure do you desire?"
"This day has already passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly. Like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be in this?
The first two lines provide a direct exposition; the latter two lines employ a metaphor. This verse is from the *Udānavarga*.
At that time, a sudden surge of terrifying waves rose from the South Sea and flooded the land, causing three large fish to flow into a shallow stream. They spoke to one another, saying: "We..."
They were all in this same predicament. While the floodwaters had not yet subsided, it was advisable to swim upstream and return to the great ocean;

however, they were again obstructed by a small boat and could not pass over it. The first fish exerted all its strength and leaped over the boat, successfully crossing. The second fish relied on some grass to get past.
The third fish, its strength utterly exhausted and the water gradually receding, did not realize that death was approaching, yet it still...
Leisurely, the Buddha then spoke a verse to admonish the people of the world: "Once the limit of this day has been fixed, how can one hope for an increase?
Now that one day has passed, it is precisely one day lessened from one's future lifespan; therefore, it is said to 'decrease accordingly.
If it is thus with each day, the same applies to months and years. How can one wait until old age, only to sit by and lose one's natural span of life?"
Alas! When the water for a fish has already diminished, it is further exacerbated by the wind and the scorching sun. Yet the foolish fish, lacking awareness, swims about as if nothing were amiss.
As its old age approaches, the four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—assail it, pressing upon it day and night with a severity even greater than that of the fish in scant water.
Therefore it is said: "What joy can there be in this? If one can generate a courageous and resolute mind and remain unattached to the two extremes, [one shall escape].
Relying upon the Middle Way, one practices and realizes the perfect non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, suddenly attaining accord with the unborn.

Thus one transcends the stream of the two deaths and returns to the original source of truth. It is like a fish exerting all its strength to leap over a boat; yet, if one’s faculties are insufficient, this may not be possible.
One should immediately practice according to the teachings and realize the principle of true emptiness, traversing the various stages and emerging from the stream of birth and death.
This is like a fish relying on a boat to pass safely from head to tail along the edge of the grass.

If, however, one is indolent and fails to seek advancement, merely coveting the minor desires and pleasures of humans and devas while failing to perceive that impermanence is approaching, one is truly like a foolish fish in shallow water.
Third, performing the preliminary procedures (*pūrvakaraṇīya*):
Is the Saṃgha assembled?
Whenever one performs a *karmavācanā* or a *poṣadha*, before undertaking any formal monastic procedure (*dharmakarma*), one must invariably carry out these six preliminary methods.

Only then can it be accomplished. Therefore, all monks within the same boundary must assemble together in one place with both body and mind, in order to prevent the expedient means of schism through a separate assembly.
Thus, he now first asks; if they have assembled, one should answer, "They have assembled."
Are you in harmony? Is there a single Dharma-affair? Are you assembled together in one place? You must have no dispute in thought or word. Those who do not attend must grant their consent (*chanda*).

Although it was previously said that they should gather like clouds, one must still guard against the causes and conditions of strife which would obstruct the Dharma-affair; therefore, this question is asked next. If...
"Is there concord? One should answer, "There is concord.
"The Sangha is assembled in concord; what is being done?

This refers to the fact that the Sangha has now assembled in concord. As for what *dharma*-activity is being performed, such activities are not of one kind; however, they are all entrusted [to the assembly].

The Sangha must gauge what is appropriate; therefore, it is necessary to question the individual concerning their actions before the assembly. When performing the *poṣadha*, one should respond by saying, "I shall recite the precepts for the *poṣadha*.
If it is not the time for the *poṣadha*, one should state the matter according to the specific circumstance. Alternatively, after the assembly has gathered, one may further add a single [formula].
Once the *jñapti-karman* has been performed, one then calls the śrāmaṇera-bodhisattva to enter.

How could one know that the bodhisattva’s great precepts universally encompass all beings, both human and non-human, and are not restricted solely to the Saṃgha? Therefore, it is not called the *śīla-deśanā-karman*, but rather the *śīla-deśanā-poṣadha*.
Thus, at the time of receiving the bodhisattva precepts, there is likewise no *karman*; it is performed only in the presence of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas.

To perform the threefold prostration before the image of the Bodhisattva is itself the *karmavācanā*. When the community of bhikṣus performs various ritual acts (*karmavastu*), it should be done at another time;
specifically, after the Bodhisattva-bhikṣus have performed the *poṣadha*, one must exclude those who have not received full ordination before the *karmavācanā* may be carried out.
Among these, those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts and those who are impure do not emerge.

This excludes two types of persons: first, those who have not yet received the great precepts of the *cittotpāda* (the arousal of the bodhicitta); second, those who, having previously received them, have committed an offense. There are two kinds of offenses:

first, committing one of the ten grave transgressions (*daśa-guru-dharma*) without yet having seen a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*); second, committing a minor defilement (*laghu-mala*) without yet having [confessed] before [a witness].

First, one should perform repentance. In no case should one allow such a person to participate in the *poṣadha* ceremony; they must immediately be expelled from the assembly and placed beyond the range of sight and hearing.
If there is no such person, one should respond by saying: "In this assembly, there is no one who has not received the bodhisattva precepts, nor is there anyone who is impure."
Regarding those who do not attend and must entrust their *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purity):
how many people declare their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*? If there are none, one should answer: "In this assembly, there is no one who declares *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*.

If there are any, they should be declared in accordance with the Dharma as follows. "Those who do not attend" means those who have not come to the place of the gathering. "Entrusting" refers to the community of monks...
In performing any ritual activity of the Dharma, it is essential that both body and mind be fully assembled to achieve true harmony.

Even if one has personal affairs concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, or matters such as illness or nursing the sick, one may then open the mind for assembly and permit the transmission through mind and speech.
Only when one performs the tasks for which the Saṃgha has been convened can both parties' objectives be accomplished;
thus, it does not hinder the Dharma-activity, nor does it incur the fault of being a separate assembly. To "declare one's desire" (chanda) means to declare one’s intention:

"Regarding the legal Saṃgha-affairs to be performed by the Saṃgha, my heart desires to rejoice in and participate in them together. However, due to a certain circumstance, I am unable to attend the assembly. One should then entrust [one's representation] accordingly.
It is conferred upon one person, transmitted from mind and mouth, and then recited within the assembly. One may speak thus to the person receiving the entrustment:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the Bodhisattva-precept bhikṣu [Name], regarding this legal matter of the Saṃgha, grant my consent and purity" (recite once).
If one is too ill to speak, one should manifest signs through the body or hands. This is how the entrustment is received.
A person, holding the *chanda* (consent) to bring it into the midst of the Saṃgha, immediately assumes the proper deportment and replies: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
I, the Bodhisattva-precept monk [Name], have received from him the *chanda* for purity. Regarding that legal matter of the Saṃgha, I grant the *chanda* for purity" (stated once).
If it is not the time for the *poṣadha*, when the Saṃgha performs various *karmas* and formal acts, one simply omits the two words "purity."

[The term] *śuddhi* (purity). Now, one may not grant purity alone. Because at the time of the *poṣadha*, the Saṃgha may perform various ritual acts, it is necessary to grant both the desire (*chanda*) and the purity.
Only when one is personally free from offenses and pure is the *poṣadha* permitted.
○ Fourth: Reciting the Preface to the Precepts.
All you sons of the Buddhas, join your palms and listen with a sincere mind. I now wish to recite the preface to the Great Precepts of all Buddhas. As the assembly has gathered, listen in silence.
If you know yourselves to have committed offenses, you should repent and confess them. Through repentance and confession, there is peace and joy; if you do not repent, your offenses will increase.
Deeply. Those who are free from offense remain silent. By your silence, it should be known that the assembly is pure.
Venerable sirs, laymen and laywomen, listen attentively.
There are two matters for listening: first, to listen with palms joined in reverence and sincerity; second, to grant permission to listen with faultless purity.

"All you sons of the Buddha" refers to the fourfold assembly of sons of the Buddha present here who are listening to the precepts. Regarding "the introductory sequence of the great precepts of all Buddhas":
this Mind-Ground Precept is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have spoken in common; it transcends the Two Vehicles. Therefore—

This is called the Great Precepts (*mahā-śīla*). "Preface" (*xu*) means "introduction" (*xu*); it serves as the introduction to this scripture consisting of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
There are two requirements for the assembly: first, that the physical bodies gather together in one place; second, that they listen silently with a sincere mind.
Regarding repentance leading to peace and happiness: if one knows that one has committed an offense, one should, before the *poṣadha*, act according to the Dharma.

One must confess one's transgressions openly before permission is granted to hear the precepts. Through confession, the body and mind become pure in the present life, thereby attaining peace and happiness;
in future lives, one will not fall into the three miserable realms and shall eventually attain the great bliss of Nirvana.

If one does not confess and instead conceals the fault for even a single night, one incurs a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*); thus it is said that the sin becomes increasingly grave. [From] the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*.
*Upāsaka* means "lay devotee" (near-service man); *upāsikā* means "lay devotee" (near-service woman).
These are those who have received the five precepts. If one has not yet received the five precepts, one must not be granted the Bodhisattva precepts.
When reciting the precepts, one must use a clear voice with each syllable distinct, neither too slow nor too fast; one should not chant or sing in a drawn-out tone.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the age of the final dharma, one should revere the prātimokṣa.
The prātimokṣa is precisely these precepts. When upholding these precepts, it is like encountering light in the darkness, or like a poor person finding a treasure.
It is like a sick person who has recovered, like a prisoner released from jail, or like a traveler who has returned home;
you should know that this is none other than our Great Teacher, even though the Buddha is not dwelling in the world.

He charged [his disciples] that in the Final Dharma (mofa), they should revere the precepts as their teacher. The Buddha-dharma has three periods: the True Dharma (zhengfa), the Semblance Dharma (xiangfa), and the Final Dharma.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the first millennium is called the True Dharma; during this time, those who receive the teachings are able to practice and can immediately realize the fruits [of the path].
The second millennium is called the Semblance Dharma. "Semblance" (xiang) means "resembling"; it refers to the existence of the teachings.

There was the period of Practice (*pratipatti*), which resembled the time of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). During that time, people who received the teachings were able to practice them, yet for the most part they could not realize the fruits [of the path].
Once the True and Semblance periods had passed, we now dwell in the Age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*). Although people receive the teachings, for the most part they cannot practice;
and even if they can practice, they cannot realize the fruits. The older edition reads "Semblance Dharma" (*saddharmapratirūpaka*); this refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Three thousand years have passed; it is no longer that time, and therefore this has been revised. *Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "Guarantee of Liberation.
This means that it guarantees practitioners will attain liberation from birth and death, thereby realizing the state of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

The rest is as explained in the commentary. This precept is the great torch of the Dharma; it can shatter the dark abode of sentient beings' afflictions, and is thus like meeting with light in the darkness.

This precept is fully endowed with immeasurable merit and the wealth of the Dharma, serving as the provisions for the merit and wisdom of Bodhisattvas, and is thus like a poor person finding treasure. This precept can cure the three poisons of sentient beings.
Because it is the retribution for karmic offenses, it is like a sick person obtaining recovery. This precept possesses the wondrous function of all liberations;
it can eliminate the suffering of sentient beings bound in the prison of the triple world, and is thus like a prisoner released from jail.
This precept can cause the long eons of saṃsāra to cease for sentient beings, leading them into the great city of nirvāṇa, and is thus like a long-distance traveler.
"Attaining refuge. These five metaphors praise the efficacy of the precepts. "The Great Master" refers to Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata was approaching parinirvāṇa, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "While the Tathāgata remains in the world, we take the Buddha as our teacher."
"When the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, what shall one take as teacher? The Buddha said, "One should rely upon the *prātimokṣa* as teacher.
Therefore it is said: "Know that this precept is the Great Teacher of the assembly. If one can now honor the precepts and practice them, it is no different from the Buddha being present in the world.
The *Yishu* states: "The Bodhisattva precepts are the opening chapter for the mobilization of goodness."

It is the vanguard for repelling evil and the direct path for returning to the source. If the origin of birth can be exhausted, even those of the Śrāvaka’s minor practices still cherish and revere the Prātimokṣa;
how much more so should a Bodhisattva, possessing dual concern for self and others, not maintain the precepts with meticulous care? Both the internal and external paths alike honor and uphold them;
kings, ministers, and the common people all submit themselves with reverent devotion. This is indeed the supreme cause for attaining the ultimate fruit.
This is the sublime practice of establishing the *maṇḍala*; therefore, one should revere it as no different from the Buddha himself.
A sense of dread is difficult to arouse, and a virtuous mind is difficult to generate. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Do not disregard even a minor offense, thinking there will be no calamity.

Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel. To commit a transgression in a single instant brings the calamity of falling into the Avīci Hell. Once one loses this human body, ten thousand..."
The kalpas do not return;
this is the meaning of the preceding verse from the *Dharmapada*. It is provided so that one may recognize that cause and effect are unfailing.

The mind that fears transgression is difficult to arouse, and the mind that delights in goodness is difficult to bring forth. The analogy of the falling drop illustrates that even a small offense must not be treated lightly; through the accumulation of small acts, much is produced.

It fills his body and mind, like a large vessel filled to the brim. Therefore, when a bodhisattva upholds the prohibitive precepts, whether they be minor or grave offenses, he maintains them with reverence and firmness, making no distinction between them.
In the Sanskrit language, *kṣaṇa* means "one thought-moment" (*ekacitta-ksana*); it is the shortest possible duration of time.
For example, in the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers, there are sixty-five *kṣaṇas*. One *kṣaṇa*...
Within this interval, there are nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing; that is to say, the extreme swiftness with which one commits transgressions and the long duration of their retribution.

One falls into the Avīci Hell and suffers for many kalpas. Upon emerging from hell, one again falls among the hungry ghosts and animals, transmigrating through the three realms and circling through the six paths.
Undergoing thousands of births and ten thousands of deaths, one fails to obtain a human body; hence it is said: "ten thousand kalpas."
It does not remain;
the vigor of youth does not endure, like a galloping horse. Human life is impermanent, passing away faster than water over a mountain torrent.
Though one exists today, tomorrow is difficult to guarantee.
The physical strength and complexion of youth decline day by day; they do not remain still for even a single *kṣaṇa*.
Thus, they are like a white colt passing through a crevice, or like a swift horse galloping away. "Impermanence" (*anityatā*) carries the meaning of shifting flux and lack of abiding.
Human life migrates and changes from moment to moment, its swiftness exceeding that of a mountain torrent. Since it is impermanent, one must call out—
The breath is difficult to fathom; moreover, who can guarantee that it will remain tomorrow?
Therefore, all of you, with single-mindedness, diligently seek progress; be careful not to be indolent or lazy, nor to yield to sleep and self-indulgence.
At night, you should immediately collect the mind and maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem; do not let it pass in vain, for to labor in vain will lead to deep regret in later generations.
All of you, each with a single-minded focus, should reverently rely upon these precepts and practice according to the Dharma; this is how you should train.

First, each person must be single-minded. This is an exhortation to practice with diligence and not let the passing time go to waste. During the day, one should recite and study the Sūtras and Vinaya.

During the first and last watches of the night, one should collect the mind and practice seated meditation (*dhyāna*). If one wishes to rest during the middle watch of the night, one must not indulge oneself in sleep, for it gives rise to many faults.
One should instead maintain mindfulness and fix the thoughts upon the names of the Triple Gem, so that transgressions may be extinguished.
"Merit-born" means being free from all faults. "Vainly" means emptily. During the day, the six sense-faculties rush outward, engaging with various dusty realms;
this is called "exhaustion. At night, the body and mind become weary and sluggish; this is called "fatigue.

Such exhaustion and fatigue are not only empty efforts that yield no benefit, but also cause the transgressions of the three karmas to accumulate daily. One will inevitably fall into the three miserable paths and must thereafter feel deep regret.
There is no way to reach it; therefore, it is said that those of later generations will deeply regret it.

"Each with a single mind" means to admonish one to be careful regarding body and mind, to practice according to these true precepts, to study with diligent effort, and to maintain them as they were taught without being distracted by other thoughts;
hence, it is called "single-mindedness."

○ Fifth, the interrogation of the venerable ones: Today, on the tenth (or fifth, or fourteenth) day of the bright or dark fortnight, we shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the Bodhisattva precepts. The assembly should listen with a single mind.
Those who have transgressions should confess them; those without transgressions should remain silent. By remaining silent, it shall be known that the venerable ones are pure.
It is pure. One is fit to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. The introduction to the Bodhisattva precepts has now been concluded. I now ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this regard? (Three times.)
If one has committed a minor offense (*laghu-mala*) but did not previously recall the transgression and only remembers it upon the third inquiry, one must immediately disclose it before the assembly.
Only after having repented and become pure is one fit to hear the precepts. If one knows [the offense] yet remains silent, one further commits the offense of intentional lying.
Therefore, during the three inquiries, one should properly examine oneself in a mirror or repent before the assembly, lest [further faults] be incurred.
If the *poṣadha* ceremony is being held in a noisy or chaotic manner, one should immediately confess the offense committed to one's neighbor in the seat, or alternatively, reflect upon it mentally.

Once the *poṣadha* has concluded, one must perform the repentance according to the Dharma. Only by doing so may one hear the precepts. This applies even if one recalls having committed one of the ten grave offenses (*daśa-ānantarya*).

One should immediately rise from one's seat and go outside the assembly. Once the assembly has finished the *poṣadha*, one must approach a person who knows the Dharma and confess everything with all one’s heart, weeping and shedding tears, requesting instruction on the method for extinguishing the offense.

To remain silent signifies that one is pure. [Question: Above this, there are various praises of the efficacy of the precepts; why are they not recorded here? [Answer: Because they have already been briefly provided above in the section on taking refuge and within the *Śīlaskandha-uddāna* (Preface to the Precepts).

In this present age of the Dharma’s decline, the minds of ordinary people are largely indolent; they prefer the simple and loathe the complex. Furthermore, fearing that the recitation of the precepts might be delayed, I have not recorded [the detailed explanations].
Venerable sirs, since you remain silent, you are pure in this matter. Thus shall this be upheld.
"Regarding this matter, 'thus it is maintained' means to maintain it with full comprehension and without forgetfulness. Having been interrogated three times, the assembly is pure.
Because they are pure, they remain silent. By their silence, I now comprehend and remember this matter as being thus;
knowing the assembly to be pure, I am fit to recite the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra. Question: What was recited previously?

[The sequence is: first the preface to the precepts (*śīla-uddeśa*) and so forth; next, the assembly of the *saṃgha* and the inquiry for concord (*sāmīcī-pṛcchā*); and finally, the interrogation regarding subsequent matters. Why, then, is the assembly gathered first now, followed by the recitation of the preface to the precepts?
Answer: Because the old text was inverted and its meaning was not in accord with the logic. Since the preface constitutes the introduction to the entire scripture, [it must come first].

Having finished reciting the introduction, one should immediately interrogate regarding purity and then recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Furthermore, having assembled the Saṃgha, one asks what is to be done;
this is just as in the *poṣadha* of the bhikṣus: first one recites the verses of praise, next one assembles the Saṃgha;

once assembled, one performs the *jñapti-karman*; having finished the motion, one recites the introduction; having finished the introduction, one interrogates; having interrogated, one then recites the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.

Now, based on the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra*, following those hymns of praise, and also according to the sequence of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya Prātimokṣa, I shall encourage the practice of gathering the Saṃgha;
the only difference here is the absence of the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), which serves merely to briefly indicate the knowledge of the lunar dates,
both waxing and waning.
6. Correctly Reciting the Precept Sūtra:
This refers to reciting from the lower portion of the "Mind-Ground" chapter (*Cittabhūmi-paṭala*), beginning from the words "At that time" up to "together attaining the Buddha-way.
If there are difficult circumstances, one should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, which should be stated as: "The Ten Grave Prātimokṣa. Now...
When it comes to reciting the minor precepts of light defilement, one should say: "The forty-eight minor precepts shall now be recited.

In this manner, one should recite the full texts of each of the fifty-eight precepts. Furthermore, fearing that difficult circumstances may soon arise, one should briefly recite the full texts of five or six of the ten major precepts;
for the remaining major and minor precepts, it is also permissible to recite only the title of each precept. Thus, in various regions today...

In the assembly hall, the community generally recites the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* in the forenoon and performs the *poṣadha* ceremony in the afternoon, briefly reciting the names and categories of the precepts.

However, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions perform the *poṣadha*. If the time for continuous recitation is pressing, one may recite the Bhikṣu-precepts in the forenoon and the Bodhisattva-precepts in the afternoon.
Alternatively, if it is difficult to assemble a large number of people, one may perform the ceremony on the fourteenth day.
The Buddha established the *poṣadha*. On the fifteenth day, the Bodhisattva performs the *poṣadha*.
Having finished reciting the precepts, he descends from his seat and addresses the assembly, saying:

"I, [Name], respectfully thank the great assembly. Appointed by the Sangha to recite the precepts, my three karmas were not diligent; the text of the precepts was stiff and dry, and I sat for a long time."
Postponed. May it cause no distress to sentient beings. We look forward to the compassion of the assembly and their joyful acceptance of this offering.
Attached: A Commentary on the Ritual for Reciting the Bodhisattva Precepts (End). Phonetic Glossary.
The faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors: the faculties are the five faculties; the powers are the five powers; enlightenment refers to the seven factors of enlightenment;
and the path refers to the eightfold noble path. These are explained in detail elsewhere.
The "two deaths" refer to the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), as explained in the commentary.
*Vibhūti* is translated here as "Guangzhou" (Broad State);
*ratna* is translated here as "Jewel" (*bao*).
Gayāśīrṣa is translated here as Elephant Forest (Gajavana).
Mahā is translated here as Great.
Bodhi was formerly translated as Enlightenment (Pútí).
*Citta* is translated here as "mind" (*xin*).
*Śramaṇa* is translated as "merit" (*gōngláo*), or alternatively as "diligent practice," because one diligently practices to attain *nirvāṇa*.

It is also called "the one who has stilled the mind. The *Sūryodgama-sūtra* (Ruìyìng jīng) states: "One who stills the mind reaches the fundamental source; therefore, he is called a *śramaṇa*. — *Āgama*.
The Sūtra says: Having renounced affection and love, one leaves the household life to cultivate the Way. One restrains and governs the sense faculties, remaining unstained by external desires.
With a mind of universal compassion, one does nothing harmful. Encountering joy, one does not rejoice; meeting with suffering, one does not grieve. One is able to endure like the earth.
Therefore, he is called a śramaṇa.

The character *qū* (pronounced like *chí*) means to run or hasten. In common usage, the *qū* of "hastening" (*bēn-qū*) is taken to be the same as the *qū* of "advancing" (*jìn-qū*), but this is incorrect.
